relationship: Loss of faithful people
rationale: The psalm laments the disappearance of the holy one and the scarcity of truth among people. Micah likewise laments the loss of the devout person and the absence of upright conduct; both describe a social crisis of faithfulness.

relationship: Deceit toward a neighbor
rationale: The psalm joins empty speech to a neighbor with deceitful lips and a heart-and-heart formulation. Jeremiah makes the outward and inward discrepancy explicit: peaceful words to a neighbor conceal enmity within.

relationship: Judgment upon deceitful and arrogant lips
rationale: Both prayers seek an end to deceitful lips associated with arrogant speech. Psalm 11 asks for their destruction, while Psalm 30 asks that they become speechless and specifies their attacks on the righteous.

relationship: The boasting and unrestrained tongue
rationale: The speakers magnify their tongue and claim that their lips have no lord. James describes the tongue boasting great things and being untamable by humans; the texts expose dangerous claims and effects of speech rather than endorsing its independence.

relationship: Divine action in response to oppression and cries
rationale: The Lord announces that He will arise because of poor people's misery and needy people's groaning. In Exodus He explicitly connects seeing Israel's affliction and hearing its cry with coming down to rescue it; the shared response pattern occurs in different settings.

relationship: Divine words refined by fire
rationale: The Lord's sayings are compared with silver tested by fire and purified sevenfold. Proverbs likewise calls all God's words refined by fire, giving a particular counterpart to the psalm's refining image.

relationship: The hidden face and apparent forgetting
rationale: Both laments combine God's turning His face away with forgetting the afflicted speaker or community. Psalm 12 asks how long this will continue, while Psalm 43 asks why it occurs.

relationship: Death described as sleep
rationale: The prayer asks for light to the eyes lest the speaker fall asleep into death. Jesus calls Lazarus asleep, and the narrative explicitly explains that He means Lazarus's death; the shared image is death as sleep, in distinct situations.

relationship: Preventing an enemy's triumphant boast
rationale: The speaker fears an enemy saying that he prevailed and afflicters rejoicing at a fall. Psalm 34 similarly asks that enemies not rejoice or claim to have swallowed the speaker, making hostile boasting the specific shared concern.

relationship: Exultation and praise to the Most High's name
rationale: The closing promise to exult and sing praise to the Lord Most High's name corresponds to Psalm 9's explicit sequence of rejoicing, exulting and praising the Most High's name. Psalm 12 additionally grounds its response in mercy and salvation.

relationship: Parallel fool and corruption stanza
rationale: Both passages place the denial of God in a fool's heart and follow it with corruption, abominable conduct and the absence of kindness or good action. Psalm 13 includes the title in its actual source unit; Psalm 52 gives the parallel statement after its separate title.

relationship: God looks from heaven for understanding and seeking
rationale: Both passages picture God looking or bending down from heaven toward humanity to see whether anyone understands or seeks Him. This is a close correspondence of the action, viewpoint and two objects of inquiry.

relationship: Parallel opening indictment
rationale: The opening of this expanded source unit closely matches Psalm 52's turning aside, becoming useless and absence of anyone doing good. Psalm 13 continues with a much longer catalogue that is absent from the short target unit.

relationship: Extended shared indictment text
rationale: The complete source unit includes the turned-aside, open-tomb, asp-venom, cursing, bloodshed, ruined-way, lost-peace and absent-fear catalogue also found in Romans. Romans places this sequence within an indictment of Jews and Greeks under sin; the comparison establishes the supplied texts' correspondence without deciding a direction of textual dependence.

relationship: People devoured like bread
rationale: Both passages portray lawless people consuming God's people as a meal of bread and failing to call upon God. The shared devouring simile and neglected invocation make this a particular parallel.

relationship: Fear where there was no fear
rationale: The distinctive fear-where-no-fear phrase occurs in both passages. Psalm 13 recounts their cowering and says God is with a righteous generation; Psalm 52 anticipates great fear and adds the scattering of people-pleasers' bones, so their explanations remain distinct.

relationship: Salvation from Zion and returned captivity
rationale: Both endings ask who will give Israel salvation from Zion, then join the Lord's reversal of captivity with Jacob's exultation and Israel's joy. Psalm 13 exhorts them to rejoice, while Psalm 52 states that they will do so.

relationship: Who may enter the holy mountain
rationale: Both psalms introduce qualifications for approaching the Lord with a question about His mountain and holy dwelling or place. The shared entrance question supplies the setting for their ensuing descriptions of conduct.

relationship: Moral qualifications for the holy place
rationale: The answer concerning blameless conduct, righteousness and truth in the heart corresponds to the other entrance psalm's innocent hands and pure heart. Both make inward and outward integrity relevant to the preceding question about God's holy place.

relationship: Deceit and harm to one's neighbor
rationale: The psalm excludes deceitful speech and evil against a neighbor. Leviticus prohibits going deceitfully among the people and conspiring against a neighbor's blood, providing a specific legal counterpart to the neighboring-person ethics of the entrance psalm.

relationship: Keeping one's sworn word
rationale: The psalm commends one who swears to his neighbor and does not set it aside. Numbers requires a person who swears an oath not to profane his word but to do what comes from his mouth; this comparison concerns the source unit's oath-keeping clause.

relationship: Refusal to charge interest on a loan
rationale: The worshiper's refusal to lend silver at interest corresponds to the law against placing interest upon a loan to a poor brother. The psalm gives a personal qualification, while Exodus specifies the protected borrower.

relationship: Gifts used against innocent people
rationale: The psalm rejects taking gifts against innocent people. Deuteronomy curses the person who takes a bribe to kill an innocent life, supplying a particular counterpart to the combination of payment and harm to the innocent.

relationship: God does not need human provision
rationale: The speaker addresses the Lord as having no need of his good things. Paul similarly says that the Creator is not served by human hands as though He needed anything, because He Himself gives life and everything.

relationship: The Lord as portion and inheritance
rationale: The psalm names the Lord as the speaker's portion and inheritance. In Numbers the Lord explicitly tells Aaron that He is Aaron's portion and inheritance; the shared language does not make the psalmist a holder of Aaron's land restriction.

relationship: Measured allotment and inheritance
rationale: The psalm describes measuring cords falling in excellent places for an inheritance. Joshua recounts an inheritance awarded to daughters and a measured allotment that fell to them; the concrete allotment language illuminates the psalm's image without identifying the properties.

relationship: Explicit quotation of the Lord at the right hand
rationale: Peter introduces David's words concerning Jesus and quotes the Lord continually before the speaker and at his right hand so that he is not shaken. The actual target identifies the application; the shared words are explicitly presented as David's saying.

relationship: Explicit quotation of joy and the flesh's hope
rationale: Peter's quotation repeats the rejoicing heart, exulting tongue and flesh dwelling in hope. The surrounding speech applies the quoted passage to Jesus' resurrection.

relationship: Explicit quotation of Hades and corruption
rationale: Peter's quotation repeats the refusal to abandon the soul to Hades or allow the Holy One to see decay. His subsequent explanation in Acts 2:29-32 distinguishes David's death from Jesus' resurrection.

relationship: Quotation and explanation of the Holy One's decay
rationale: Paul quotes the holy-one and decay clause and immediately distinguishes David, who saw decay, from the One God raised, who did not. This target explicitly states the resurrection application of the quoted words.

relationship: Explicit quotation of life's paths and gladness
rationale: Peter's quotation repeats God's making known life's paths and filling the speaker with gladness in His presence. The psalm additionally speaks of pleasures at God's right hand for ever, which the quoted target does not repeat.

relationship: Prayer heard in relation to integrity
rationale: The speaker asks God to hear a prayer that does not come from deceitful lips. Psalm 65 connects God's hearing with the speaker's rejection of regarding injustice in his heart; both prayers relate their hearing to integrity rather than merely repeating a request for attention.

relationship: Judgment from God and uprightness
rationale: The speaker seeks judgment from God's presence and upright things before his own eyes. Psalm 7 asks the Lord to judge according to the speaker's righteousness and names God as examiner of hearts and savior of the upright.

relationship: The heart tested by fire
rationale: The speaker reports God's testing his heart and trying him by fire. Psalm 25 asks the Lord to test the speaker and try his kidneys and heart by fire; the correspondence preserves the difference between a reported test and a requested one.

relationship: Steps directed by God
rationale: The prayer asks for steps to be firmly set in God's paths so that they are not shaken. Psalm 118 asks God to direct the speaker's steps according to His saying; both use directed steps for faithful conduct.

relationship: Divine rescue and the opposing enemies of God's right hand
rationale: The psalm addresses God as rescuing those who hope in Him from opponents of His right hand. The sea song celebrates that same divine right-hand image as strong and shattering enemies, without identifying the opponents or rescues as one event.

relationship: Guarding as the pupil of an eye
rationale: The psalm asks to be guarded as the pupil of an eye. The song in Deuteronomy uses the same protective image for the Lord's keeping Jacob in the wilderness.

relationship: Shelter under God's wings
rationale: The psalm asks for shelter under God's wings. Boaz blesses Ruth as one who has come to trust under the Lord's wings; the repeated shelter image is applied to distinct persons.

relationship: A concealed lion as the image of an attacker
rationale: The enemies are compared with a hunting lion and a young lion in hiding places. Psalm 9 likewise describes an attacker lurking like a lion in its enclosure to seize a poor man; the shared predatory ambush is more specific than hostility alone.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both headings assign the song to David and locate it at the Lord's rescue from all his enemies and Saul. The psalm adds its liturgical heading and description of David as the Lord's servant.

relationship: Confessed love and the command to love the Lord
rationale: David's song opens with his declaration that he will love the Lord. Deuteronomy commands love for the Lord with the whole heart, soul and strength; the comparison relates the expressed devotion to that explicit command, while the psalm calls the Lord himself its speaker's strength.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both song openings accumulate refuge, rescue and protection titles for the Lord, including the distinctive horn of salvation. The psalm's single unit corresponds to two Samuel units and retains its own foundation and supporter wording.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines join calling upon the praised Lord with being saved from enemies. The psalm says praising I will call, while Samuel describes the Lord as worthy of praise.

relationship: The pangs of death and divine rescue
rationale: The song describes the birth pangs of death surrounding its speaker. Peter says God raised Jesus by releasing Him from the pangs of death; the shared death-pangs image occurs in David's rescue song and an explicit resurrection announcement.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine surrounding death imagery with torrents of lawlessness. The psalm names birth pangs of death and turmoil; Samuel names crushings of death and being stunned.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: The corresponding lines depict encirclement and threatening death. The psalm specifically names Hades' birth pangs and death's traps, whereas Samuel names death's birth pangs and harsh assaults.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines connect distress, calling to God, His temple and the cry entering His ears. The psalm recounts a past call and hearing before anticipating the cry's entry; Samuel uses future forms for calling and hearing.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines describe the earth shaking because God is angry, accompanied by disturbed foundations. The psalm names the mountains' foundations, while Samuel names heaven's foundations and their being torn apart.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines join divine anger, rising smoke, fire and kindled coals. The psalm's fire comes from God's face and sets things ablaze; Samuel places it at His mouth and says it will devour.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both forms of the song depict God bending heaven, coming down and having darkness beneath His feet. The corresponding actions and position of the darkness establish the close parallel.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines portray God mounted or seated upon cherubim and flying with the wind's wings. The psalm repeats flying, whereas Samuel says He appeared upon those wings.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines make darkness God's surrounding hiding place and tent, with dark waters and clouds of air. The shared arrangement of tent, darkness, water and cloud is particular to this corresponding divine-appearance portrait.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines associate radiance before God with coals of fire. The psalm also names passing clouds and hail, while Samuel specifically says that coals were kindled from the brightness.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines pair the Lord's thunder from heaven with the Most High's giving His voice. Their parallel phrasing explicitly links heavenly thunder and the divine voice.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines depict divine arrows scattering opponents and lightning throwing them into confusion. The psalm additionally speaks of multiplying lightning flashes.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines uncover the inhabited world's foundations at the Lord's rebuke and the blast of His anger. The psalm names springs of waters and the spirit of that anger; Samuel names sea outlets and its breath.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines describe action from on high that takes the speaker out of many waters. The psalm says God sent and took him to Himself; Samuel says He reached and drew him out.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines name powerful enemies and haters who had grown stronger than the speaker. The psalm anticipates rescue with will rescue, whereas Samuel reports that He rescued him.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines put an enemy encounter in the speaker's day of affliction or distress and state that the Lord became his support. The combination of timing and divine support supplies the close correspondence.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines recount being brought into a spacious place and connect rescue with God's desire or delight. The psalm anticipates rescue and adds powerful enemies and haters, whereas Samuel reports completed rescue in this unit.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines connect repayment with the speaker's righteousness and clean hands. The psalm uses will repay; Samuel reports repaid. These remain the song speaker's claims, not an independent judgment about every act in David's life.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines explain the preceding claim by keeping the Lord's ways and not acting impiously through departure from God. Their matching statement concerns the speaker's declared conduct.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines place God's judgments before the speaker and deny putting away or turning from His ordinances. The psalm says the judgments are before him; Samuel says they were.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines anticipate blamelessness toward God and guarding against the speaker's own lawlessness. The shared future orientation is preserved rather than converted into a claim of completed lifelong sinlessness.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines anticipate the Lord's repayment according to righteousness and the purity or cleanness of the speaker's hands before His eyes. This corresponds to the later, future-form statement in each song.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines pair God's showing Himself holy toward the holy with a second correspondence toward an upright person. The psalm calls the second person innocent, while Samuel uses complete; those actual terms remain distinct.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines pair chosen with chosen and twisted or crooked with a corresponding divine response. This particular two-part formulation supplies the parallel without substituting a different description of the persons.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine saving a lowly or poor people with lowering arrogant or haughty eyes. The same reversal of the lowly and proud appears in the corresponding place in the songs.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines join the Lord with a lamp and the lighting of the speaker's darkness. The psalm says the Lord will light his lamp; Samuel directly calls the Lord his lamp before anticipating light in darkness.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines explicitly attribute passing over a wall to God. The first clauses differ: the psalm anticipates rescue from a raiding band, while Samuel says the speaker will run lightly armed.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine God's blameless way, His word tested or refined by fire, and protection for those who rely on Him. These three linked assertions correspond despite the different titles and wording for strength and protection.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines use two questions to exclude rivals to the Lord and our God. The psalm repeats God, while Samuel asks about the mighty and a Creator; their actual predicates are not made identical.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines attribute the speaker's power and blameless way to God. The psalm uses girding and making the way blameless, while Samuel uses strengthening and shaking the way free.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines compare the speaker's feet with a deer's and place him upon heights. The paired foot-and-height image forms a close correspondence within the rescue songs.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines describe God training hands for war and then mention an arm and bronze bow. The psalm says God made the arms a bronze bow; Samuel says He broke a bronze bow with the speaker's arm, so the actions are distinct.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines recount God giving the protection or defence of salvation. The psalm adds right-hand support and discipline that establishes and teaches; Samuel instead names God's heeding that made the speaker great.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines associate room for the speaker's steps with secure movement. The psalm says the footprints did not grow weak, while Samuel says the legs did not shake.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines anticipate pursuing enemies and refusing to turn back before their defeat is complete. The psalm speaks of overtaking and their failing; Samuel speaks of wiping them out and finishing them.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines anticipate enemies being pressed or crushed down, unable to stand or rise, and falling beneath the speaker's feet. The shared sequence describes their defeat in each song.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines place the speaker's war strength and opponents beneath him under God's action. The psalm reports being girded and opponents fettered; Samuel anticipates strengthening and bending attackers beneath him.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines recount God giving the speaker the backs of his enemies and destroying or putting to death those who hated him. The back-turning defeat image and the identified haters correspond.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines depict opponents crying with no helper and the Lord not listening. The psalm reports their cries in the past; Samuel anticipates their crying while retaining the statement that He did not listen.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines compare the defeat of enemies with fine dust and street mud. The psalm anticipates grinding and smoothing them away, with dust before the wind; Samuel recounts grinding and crushing, with dust of the earth.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines join rescue from conflict with peoples, leadership of nations and service from an unknown people. The psalm speaks of disputes and appointment, while Samuel speaks of battle and preservation as head.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine hearing followed by obedience with foreigners lying to the speaker. The clauses appear in opposite order, and neither is changed into a claim of sincere submission.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: The corresponding foreigner lines use different images of failure and departure. The psalm says they grew old and limped away from their paths; Samuel says they will be cast away and stumble out of enclosures.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines proclaim that the Lord lives, bless God and connect exaltation with salvation. The psalm exhorts that the God of salvation be exalted, while Samuel uses Guard language and says He will be exalted.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines attribute vengeance and authority over peoples beneath the speaker to God. The psalm says He subjected peoples, while Samuel says He disciplines them; the stated actions remain distinct.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines combine rescue from enemies, being raised above attackers and rescue from an unjust man or man of wrongs. The repeated three-part deliverance description supplies the particular correspondence.

relationship: Quotation of praise among the nations
rationale: Paul explicitly quotes the thanksgiving-among-the-nations and praise-to-God's-name wording while explaining Gentiles' glorifying God for mercy. The source line also has a parallel in 2 Samuel 22:50; this comparison does not decide between the two parallel song forms as the quotation's immediate source.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both lines promise acknowledgment or thanksgiving among the nations and singing praise to the Lord's name. Their shared words also appear in the quotation recorded in Romans 15:9.

relationship: Mercy to David's royal seed
rationale: The song ends with mercy to God's anointed, David and his seed for ever. Nathan's message promises David a royal descendant, enduring kingdom and mercy that will not be withdrawn; those specific royal-seed and mercy promises correspond to the song's conclusion.

relationship: Parallel forms of David’s rescue song
rationale: Both conclusions name great deliverance for God's king and mercy toward His anointed, explicitly David and his descendants for ever. The matching royal identity and enduring lineage formula are supplied by both texts themselves.

relationship: Creation discloses the Creator
rationale: The heavens announce God's glory and the work of His hands. Romans says God's invisible power and divinity are understood through what He made; both make created things witnesses to their Creator, using different formulations.

relationship: Quotation of the worldwide sound
rationale: Romans quotes the sound going through all the earth and words reaching the inhabited world's ends in its argument about hearing. The comparison concerns the source unit's opening clauses; its additional statement that God set His dwelling in the sun is not part of the quotation.

relationship: The bridegroom emerging from a chamber
rationale: The psalm uses the simile of a bridegroom coming out of his bridal chamber. Joel's summons to communal fasting calls the bridegroom out of his bedroom and the bride out of her bridal chamber; the comparison concerns that concrete wedding-room image rather than an identity of the subjects.

relationship: The sun's course
rationale: Following its mention of the sun, the psalm depicts movement from heaven's edge to heaven's edge and heat from which none is hidden. Ecclesiastes describes the sun rising, setting and drawing toward its place; the passages present its course in praise and in reflection on recurring activity respectively.

relationship: Divine words give understanding
rationale: The source says the Lord's testimony makes infants wise. Psalm 118 says the disclosure of His words gives light and understanding to the simple; the shared instructional effect is retained while the different descriptions of its recipients remain explicit.

relationship: Commandment as illumination
rationale: The Lord's commandment shines afar and gives light to the eyes. Proverbs calls the commandment of law a lamp and a light, giving a close counterpart to the instructional light image.

relationship: True words and righteous judgments
rationale: The source calls the Lord's judgments true and justified together, while Psalm 118 joins the truth of His words with His righteous judgments. The source attributes endurance to the fear of the Lord; the target expressly attributes it to the judgments.

relationship: Divine law valued beyond precious metal
rationale: The source values the Lord's judgments beyond gold and much precious stone. Psalm 118 similarly places the law of His mouth above thousands of gold and silver; both make divine instruction more desirable than material wealth.

relationship: Divine sayings sweeter than honey
rationale: The honey-and-honeycomb comparison for the Lord's judgments closely corresponds to Psalm 118's comparison of His sayings with honey and honeycomb in the speaker's mouth. Both use sweetness to express the delight of divine instruction.

relationship: Cleansing faults beyond present awareness
rationale: The prayer asks cleansing from hidden things while questioning who understands transgressions. Leviticus provides atonement for an unintentional offence once it becomes known, showing that lack of awareness does not remove the need for cleansing or forgiveness; the respective forms are prayer and a prescribed offering.

relationship: The speaker's meditation before God
rationale: The source anticipates pleasing sayings and continual meditation before God. Psalm 103 asks that the speaker's meditation be sweet to Him; the passages respectively express expectation and petition concerning the acceptability of the speaker's own worship.

relationship: Jacob's God hears in the day of affliction
rationale: The blessing asks that the Lord hear in the day of affliction and invokes Jacob's God. Jacob himself describes God as the One who heard him in the day of affliction, providing a specific narrative counterpart to both parts of the invocation.

relationship: Divine benefit from Zion and the sanctuary
rationale: The prayer asks for help from the sanctuary and support from Zion. Psalm 133 addresses servants in the Lord's house and declares that the Lord will bless from Zion, sharing the sanctuary setting and the stated origin of divine benefit.

relationship: Whole burnt offering and a plea for deliverance
rationale: The blessing asks that the recipient's sacrifices and whole burnt offering be remembered favorably. At Mizpah Samuel offers a whole burnt offering and cries for Israel, and the Lord hears him as the enemy approaches; this compares sacrifice joined with a plea for aid in distinct settings.

relationship: Royal petition and granted desire
rationale: The blessing asks God to grant according to the recipient's heart and fulfill his counsel. Psalm 20 reports the gift of the king's soul's desire and the wish of his lips, furnishing a corresponding statement of granted desire in another royal prayer.

relationship: Rejoicing in royal salvation
rationale: The community promises to exult in the addressed person's salvation; the closing request for the king supplies the royal context. Psalm 20 explicitly says the king will rejoice in God's power and exult in His salvation, shifting the stated rejoicer from community to king.

relationship: The anointed ruler upheld by God's hand
rationale: The source joins salvation of the Lord's anointed with the saving power of His right hand. Psalm 88 names David as God's anointed and promises support from God's hand, strength from His arm and defeat of enemies; the comparison does not identify a single battle.

relationship: Trust in horses and chariots contrasted with God
rationale: The psalm contrasts reliance on chariots and horses with the Lord's name. Isaiah condemns reliance on Egypt's horses and chariots in place of seeking Israel's Holy One, making the military means and contrasting object of trust explicit in both passages.

relationship: Prayer for rulers
rationale: The psalm asks the Lord to save His king and hear the community. The letter expressly directs petitions and intercessions for kings and people in high positions, giving an explicit instruction corresponding to this kind of royal prayer.

relationship: King and community exult in salvation
rationale: The king's promised rejoicing in God's power and salvation corresponds to the preceding royal prayer's communal promise to exult in the addressed person's salvation. The passages name different participants as rejoicing and do not require one historical occasion.

relationship: Granted desire beside a royal petition
rationale: The source reports that God granted the king's soul's desire and did not deprive him of his lips' wish. Psalm 19 asks God to grant according to the heart and fulfill counsel; the particular comparison is between petitioned and reported royal desire.

relationship: A royal crown with precious stone
rationale: The source describes a crown of precious stone placed upon the king's head. Samuel recounts a crown containing gold and precious stone being placed on David's head at Rabbah; the material and royal placement correspond, without establishing that this is the same crown or occasion.

relationship: Length of days for the king
rationale: The source reports the king asking for life and receiving length of days for the age of the age. Psalm 60 anticipates added days and years for the king across generations and his remaining before God, providing a particular royal-longevity counterpart.

relationship: Enduring royal blessing before God
rationale: The source joins enduring blessing for the king with joy in God's presence. David's prayer asks that his house be blessed and remain before God for ever; the link concerns continuing royal blessing and presence, with individual king and household distinguished.

relationship: Royal stability grounded in divine mercy
rationale: The king's hope of remaining unshaken rests on the Most High's mercy. Psalm 88 promises enduring mercy, a faithful covenant and an established royal seed and throne, giving a royal-covenant counterpart to that stated basis of confidence.

relationship: Oven imagery for fiery judgment
rationale: The source pictures enemies made like a fiery furnace and devoured by fire in the Lord's anger. Malachi depicts the coming day burning like an oven and the lawless as ignited straw; both use enclosed-fire imagery for judgment while assigning the simile to different subjects.

relationship: Fruit and offspring removed in judgment
rationale: The source predicts destruction of the enemies' fruit and seed. Hosea expressly combines Ephraim's dried roots and absent fruit with the loss of offspring, supplying a particular counterpart to the use of fruit and descendants in a judgment description.

relationship: Hostile counsel unable to stand
rationale: The enemies devise evil counsel that they cannot establish. Psalm 32 contrasts the Lord's nullifying peoples' and rulers' counsels with the permanence of His own counsel; the correspondence concerns frustrated human designs rather than an identified shared conspiracy.

relationship: Enemies made to turn their backs
rationale: The opening clause anticipates enemies being made to turn their backs. David's rescue song likewise recounts his enemies' backs being turned toward him while addressing God; only that clear shared action supplies this connection.
